Sūrat al-Nisā'

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O mankind﴾: O children of Ādam. ﴿Fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾: that is, your branches come from one origin, which is the soul of your father Ādam. ﴿And created from it its mate﴾: this is conjoined (ma'ṭūf, "conjoined to") an omitted element (maḥdhūf, "elided"). It is as if it were said: "from a single soul, He brought it into being, and created from it its mate." The meaning is: He spread you out from a single soul having this description, namely that He brought it into being from earth, and created from it its mate, Ḥawwā', from one of its ribs.

﴿And spread forth from both of them﴾ [and dispersed from Ādam and Ḥawwā' ﴿men in great number and women﴾ in great number; that is, He spread forth from the two of them the two kinds of the human species, which are the males and the females]. So He described it with a description that explains and details how they were created from it, or [it refers to] your creation. The address in ﴿O mankind﴾ is to those to whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent. The meaning is: He created you from the soul of Ādam, created from it your mother Ḥawwā', and spread forth from the two of them men in great number and women, other than you, from the past nations. ("Lil-ḥaṣr" means "for restriction," i.e., the address is restricted to the group addressed.)

If you say: what the eloquence of the composition requires is that, after the command to fear Allah, there be mention of what calls to it. How then is His creating them from a single soul, in the detailed manner He mentioned, a call to it? I say: because that is among the things that show great power, and whoever has power over the like of it has power over everything. Among the things within His power is the punishment of the disbelievers and the wicked (p-٣٢٧). Reflection on it leads to fearing the One who has power over it, and dreading His punishment. Also, it shows the abundant blessing bestowed upon them, so it is their duty to fear Him by not being ungrateful for it.

When the verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Woman was created from man, so her desire is for man, and man was created from earth, so his desire is for earth."

﴿And fear Allah, by whom you ask one another﴾: the original form is tatasā'alūna, then the tā' was assimilated into the sīn (idghām, "assimilation") after being changed into a sīn, because the tā' is close to the sīn in its whispered quality. (Tasā'alūna bihi), read with lightening (takhfīf), is [the reading] of the Kufan [reader], by omitting the second tā' because of the heaviness of two tā's coming together. The meaning: some of you ask others by Allah and by the kinship ties, "do such-and-such," as a way of appealing for compassion.

﴿And the wombs﴾: it is in the accusative (naṣb, "accusative case") as conjoined to the name of Allah, the Exalted, meaning: "and fear the wombs, not to sever them." Or [it is conjoined] to the place of the prepositional phrase (ḥarf al-jarr with its object), as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr." Or [it is] in the genitive (jarr, "genitive case"): Ḥamzah [reads it this way], conjoining a noun to a pronoun, which is weak, because the attached pronoun is like its noun attached, and the prepositional phrase is like a single thing, so it resembles conjoining to part of a word. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever over you a watcher﴾: a guardian or one who knows.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 2:

﴿And give the orphans their property﴾. That is, those whose fathers have died and who have been left alone without them. The word *yutm* (orphanhood) means being alone, and from it comes *al-durrah al-yatimah* (the unique pearl). It is said that orphanhood among humans is from the father's side, and among animals from the mother's side. The proper meaning of this term applies to both the young and the adult, since the sense of being separated from the fathers remains. However, it has become customary to call them by this name before they reach the status of men. When they become independent of a guardian and a caretaker over them, the name is no longer applied to them. The saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "There is no orphanhood after puberty" (*la yutma ba'da al-hulum*), is a teaching of the Law and not a matter of language. That is, when he has reached puberty, the rulings for children no longer apply to him. The meaning is: give the orphans their property after (p-328) puberty. He called them orphans because of the closeness of their time, once they have reached maturity, to childhood. This contains an indication that the handing over of their property should not be delayed beyond the age of puberty if sound judgment is perceived in them, and that it should be given to them before the name of orphans and children has departed from them.

﴿And do not substitute the bad for the good﴾. Do not exchange the forbidden, which is the property of the orphans, for the lawful, which is your own property. Or, do not substitute the bad matter, which is the taking of the orphans' property, for the good matter, which is preserving it and abstaining from it. The form *tafa''ul* in the sense of *istif'al* is not uncommon; from it comes *ta''ajjul* in the sense of *isti'jal* (hastening).

﴿And do not devour their property along with your own property﴾. *Ila* (along with / to) is connected to an omitted element and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: added to your property. The meaning is: do not combine them with your property in spending, until you distinguish between your property and theirs, out of carelessness about what is not lawful for you and out of treating it as equal to what is lawful.

﴿Indeed, that is a great sin﴾. Indeed, devouring it is *huban kabiran*: a great wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 4, verse 3:

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾: i.e., that you will not be equitable. *Aqsata* means he was equitable (*'adala*).

﴿with regard to the orphans﴾ [The word *yatama* (orphans) is used for females as it is for males. It is the plural of *yatima* (female orphan) and *yatim* (male orphan). As for *aytam*, it is the plural of *yatim* only.] ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾: what is lawful for you ﴿of women﴾. This is because among women there are those whom God has forbidden, such as those mentioned in the verse of prohibition. It has also been said that *ma* (what) is used here with reference to attributes, since *ma* is used for the attributes of rational beings. It is as if it had been said: "the good ones among women." Also, females among rational beings take the same status as non-rational beings. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or what your right hands possess﴾. It has been said: They did not scruple about fornication, but they scrupled about guardianship of orphans. So it was said: If you fear injustice regarding the orphans, then fear fornication, and marry what is lawful for you of women, and do not hover around the forbidden. Or: They scrupled about guardianship over the wealth of orphans, but did not scruple about taking many women, even though injustice occurs among them when they are numerous. It is as if it had been said: If you scruple about this, then scruple about that. It has also been said: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾ in marrying ﴿the orphans, then marry﴾ from among the adult women. One says: "the fruit has become good" (*tabat al-thamara*), meaning it has ripened. (p-329)

﴿two, three, or four﴾: these are indefinite (*nakirat*). They are not declined (*lam yunsarifa*) because of the two reasons of being in the form of *'adl* (an irregular form) and being descriptive (*wasf*). This is what the words of Sibawayh indicate. Their position is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "women," or from "what seems good." The implied sense is: "Marry the good ones for yourselves, numbered in this number: two and two, three and three, and four and four." If you say: What is permitted to the one marrying in plurality is to combine two, or three, or four. So what is the meaning of the repetition in *mathna wa-thulatha wa-ruba'*? I say: The address is to all of them, so the repetition is necessary so that every marrying person who wants plurality may take what number he wishes from the number that has been permitted to him. Just as you say to a group: "Divide this wealth, which is a thousand dirhams, two dirhams each, three each, and four each." If you were to use the single form, it would have no meaning. The conjunction *wa* (and) is used to indicate permission to combine the groups; if *aw* (or) were used in its place, the sense of permission would be lost.

﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly﴾ among these numbers, ﴿then one﴾: adhere to it, or choose one.

﴿or what your right hands possess﴾: in ease, it equates one free woman with slave women, without limitation.

﴿That﴾ refers to choosing one or taking concubines. ﴿is nearer to preventing you from being unjust﴾: closer to not inclining away (*tamilu*) or not oppressing (*tajuru*). It is said: *'āla al-mizan 'awlan* (the scale tilted) when it inclines, and *'āla al-hakim fi hukmihi* (the judge was unjust in his judgment) when he oppresses. It is reported from al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, that he interpreted ﴿an-la ta'ulu﴾ as "that your dependents do not increase." They objected to him, saying: One says *a'āla yu'ilu* when his dependents increase. It was answered that it may be taken from your saying: *'āla al-rajulu 'iyalahu ya'ulu-hum* (the man supported his dependents), like your saying: *mana-hum yamunu-hum* when he spent on them, because whoever has many dependents is obliged to support them. In that there is what makes it difficult for him to guard the limits of scrupulousness (*wara'*) and the earning of what is lawful. The words of one like him among the great scholars deserve to be understood in the best sense, and it should not be supposed of him that he altered *tu'ilu* to *ta'ulu*. It seems that in his interpretation of this word he followed the path of allusions (*kinayat*).

ۭ**And give the women their dowries (ṣadaqāt) as a gift (niḥlah)**. Ṣadaqāt means their dowries (muhūr). Niḥlah comes from the verb naḥala fulānun kadhā, meaning when one gives it to him and grants it to him, out of goodwill from his own soul; niḥlah and niḥl (both meaning a gift freely given). It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because niḥlah and ītāʾ (giving) carry the same meaning, as if he had said: "And bestow upon the women their dowries as a gift," i.e., give them their dowries willingly from your own hearts. Alternatively, it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) referring to the addressees, i.e., they should give them their dowries while being generous and cheerful in soul and giving. Or it is taken as a description of the dowries: given as a gift, willingly given from the goodwill of souls. It has been said: niḥlah from God Most High means a gift from Him and a favour bestowed upon them. It has also been said: niḥlah means religion (milla), as in "so-and-so professes (yantaḥilu) such-and-such," meaning he adheres to it in faith; the meaning being: give them their dowries as a matter of religious obligation (diyānah), in which case it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu). The address is to the husbands, and it has been said that it is to the guardians (awliyāʾ), because they used to take the dowries of their daughters.

**﴿Then if they give you willingly of it﴾**: to the husbands, **﴿anything of it﴾**, i.e., of the dowry, since it has the meaning of ṣadaqāt.

**﴿willingly (nafsan)﴾**: a specification (tamyīz). It is singular because the purpose is to state the category, and the singular indicates it. The meaning: if they grant you something of the dowry, and their souls are willing toward it, good and not sullied, by what the gift compels them to, owing to the harshness of your characters and the badness of your dealings with them. The verse indicates the narrowness of the path in this matter and the obligation of caution, since it makes the condition depend on the goodwill of the soul, saying: **﴿if they give you of it anything willingly﴾**, and not "if they give you," to inform that what is considered is the soul's willing relinquishment of what is given with good heart.

**﴿then consume it﴾**: the pronoun refers to "anything." **﴿with enjoyment (hanīʾan)﴾**, without sin in it, **﴿with ease (marīʾan)﴾**, without harm in it. Both were explained by the Prophet ﷺ, or: hanīʾan in this world without demand, marīʾan in the next without consequence. These two are adjectives from hanuʾa al-ṭaʿām and maruʾa, when the food is palatable and free of disturbance. They are descriptions of a verbal noun, i.e., an eating that is pleasant and easy, or a circumstantial state of the pronoun, i.e., "consume it, and it is pleasant and easy." This is an expression of emphasis in permissibility and the removal of consequence. Yazid reads hanīʾan marīʾan without hamza, and likewise Ḥamzah when pausing; the rest read them with hamza.

From ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: "If any of you feels ill in some way, let him ask his wife for three dirhams of her dowry, then let him buy honey with it, and let him mix it with rainwater, and Allah will then combine for him hanīʾan, marīʾan, shifāʾ and mubārak."

﴿And do not give the foolish their property﴾ meaning the wasteful (al-mubadhdhirin) who spend their property on what is not fitting, and who have no ability to improve it, to make it grow, or to manage it. The address is to the guardians (awliya'). He attributed the property of the foolish to the guardians by saying ﴿your property﴾, because they are in charge of it (yalunaha) and hold it (yumsikunaha).

﴿which Allah has made for you a means of support (qiyaman)﴾, that is, a means of sustenance (qiwaman) for your bodies, and a livelihood for your families and your children. (Qiyaman), meaning qiyaman, is the reading of Nafi' and al-Shami, just as ʿiwadha came in the sense of iyadhan. The original form of qiyam is qiwam, and the waw was changed to a ya' because the letter before it is kasra. The early Muslims (al-salaf) used to say: "Wealth is the weapon of the believer," and "Leaving what Allah will not hold me accountable for is better than my having to depend on people." And it is related from Sufyan, who had merchandise that he would turn over: "Were it not for it, the Banu al-Abbas would have made a plaything of me."

﴿and provide for them from it﴾, that is, make it a source of their provision, by trading with it and seeking profit, so that their maintenance comes from the profits and not from the principal, which the spending would consume. ﴿And clothe them, and speak to them a kind word﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: "It is a fine promise: If you become sound and rightly guided, we will hand over your property to you." Every statement or action that a good soul finds agreeable, whether by reason or by the Sharia, is ma'ruf (what is known and good), and whatever you reject for its ugliness is munkar (what is denounced).

﴿And test the orphans﴾ by examining their intellects, and by finding out their conditions and their competence in managing property before puberty. Testing, according to us, means handing over to the orphan what he can manage, until his state becomes clear in what results from him. It is evidence for the permissibility of permitting a sensible child to engage in trade. ﴿Until, when they reach marriageable age﴾, i.e., the wet dream (ḥulum), because he becomes fit for marriage according to him, and for pursuing what marriage is aimed at, which is procreation.

﴿If you perceive in them﴾, i.e., you find, ﴿maturity (rushd)﴾, meaning guidance in dealings and soundness in transactions,

﴿then hand over to them their property﴾ without delaying it beyond the age of puberty. The construction of this statement is that what follows "until" up to ﴿hand over to them their property﴾ is made the limit (ghāyah) of the testing. This is "ḥattā," which is followed by sentences, as in his saying:

*Until the water of the Tigris turned reddish*

The sentence that follows it is a conditional sentence, because idhā (when) carries the meaning of a condition, and the verb of the condition is "they reach marriage." His saying ﴿If you perceive in them maturity, then hand over to them their property﴾ is a sentence made of a condition and a consequent, which falls as the answer to the first condition, which is ﴿when they reach marriage﴾. It is as if it were said: test the orphans until the time of their puberty and until they become entitled to having their property handed to them, on the condition that you perceive maturity in them. The indefiniteness of "rushd" indicates that a specific kind of maturity is intended, namely maturity in disposing of property and in trade. Alternatively, it indicates diminution, i.e., a portion of maturity, so that its completeness is not awaited. This is evidence for Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, regarding handing over the property upon reaching twenty-five years of age.

﴿And do not consume it extravagantly and hastily, fearing that they will grow up﴾, i.e., do not consume it wastefully and hastening before they grow up. ﴿Israfan﴾ and ﴿bidaran﴾ are two verbal nouns in the position of circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl), and ﴿an yakburū﴾ is in the position of a verbal noun governed in the accusative by ﴿bidaran﴾. It is also permissible for them to be objects of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), i.e., because of your extravagance and your haste to their growing up, you are negligent in spending it, saying: "We spend on what we desire before the orphans grow up, so that they cannot seize it from our hands."

﴿And whoever is rich, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾. He divided the matter between the guardian being rich and the guardian being poor. The rich one abstains from consuming it, i.e., he guards himself against consuming the orphan's property. "Istaʿaffa" is a stronger form than "ʿaffa," as if he were seeking an increase in abstinence. The poor one eats a measured sustenance, cautiously in his eating. From Ibrahim: "what stills the hunger and covers the nakedness."

﴿Then when you hand over to them their property, call witnesses against them﴾, to the effect that they received and took possession of it, in order to prevent denial, and to avoid the oath being imposed on you when disputes and denials arise. ﴿And Allah is sufficient as Reckoner﴾, i.e., as one who calls to account. So adhere to truthfulness and beware of lying. Or it refers back to his saying ﴿let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾, i.e., let him not be extravagant, for Allah will call him to account for it and recompense him for it. The subject of "kafā" is the word "Allah," and the "bāʾ" is superfluous. "Kafā" transitively takes two objects, as evidenced by ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137].

(p-٣٣٢)

[(p-٣٣٣)] ﴿For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave.﴾ They are the heirs among the kindred, to the exclusion of others. ﴿Of what little or much of it﴾ is a *badal* (substitution, in grammatical terms a restatement of the preceding noun) of ﴿of what he leaves﴾, with the governing verb repeated. The pronoun in "minhu" (of it) refers back to what was left. ﴿A share﴾ is in the accusative *'ala al-ikhtisas* (accusative of specification), meaning: "I mean, a share."

﴿Obligatory﴾ means fixed, so they must take it. It is narrated that Aws ibn Thabit left his wife Umm Kuhha and three daughters, and the two sons of his paternal uncle took his inheritance away from them. The people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to women or children, and they used to say: "None inherits except one who thrusts with spears and seizes the spoils." Umm Kuhha came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained. He said: "Go back until I see what Allah brings about." Then the verse was revealed. He sent to them both: "Do not divide anything of Aws's property, for Allah, exalted is He, has assigned them a share, and He has not explained it until He explains it." Then ﴿Allah enjoins you﴾ was revealed, and he gave Umm Kuhha the eighth and the daughters the two-thirds, and the remainder went to the two sons of the paternal uncle.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 8:

﴿And when the distribution is attended by the near of kin﴾, i.e., the distribution of the estate, ﴿and the orphans and the needy﴾ from among the outsiders (those who are not heirs), ﴿then provide for them﴾, i.e., give them "from it" "out of what the parents and the near relatives have left". This is a command of recommendation (nadb), and it remains in force and has not been abrogated (nasakh, i.e., abrogation). It has also been said that it was obligatory at the beginning, and then it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance. ﴿And speak to them a kind word﴾, i.e., a fair excuse and a good promise. It has also been said that the "kind word" is that they should say to them: "Take it, may Allah bless you," and that they should belittle what they have given them and not reproach them for it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 9:

﴿And let those fear [God] who, if they left behind them weak offspring, would be anxious for them; so let them fear God and speak words of appropriate justice.﴾

The intended meaning of "them" is the guardians (al-awsiya), who were commanded to fear God, so that they would be apprehensive for those orphans (al-yatama) in their care, and so that they would show compassion toward them. He made them fear for their own offspring if they were to leave them weak, and to picture that in their own minds, so that they would not dare to act contrary to compassion and mercy. (p-334) The phrase "law" (if, lau) together with what follows it is a relative clause (silah) for "those who" (alladhina). That is: let those fear whose attribute and condition is that, if they were about to leave behind them weak offspring (and this is at the time of their dying), they would fear for them the loss (al-diya') after them, because their guardian would be gone. The answer (jawab) of "law" is "they would fear." The "appropriate speech" (al-qawl al-sadid) from the guardians is that they should speak to them as they speak to their own children, with good manners and welcome, and call them: "O my son" (ya bunayya) and "O my boy" (ya waladi).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ "unjustly" (ظالِمِينَ, ẓālimīn), so it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿They are only consuming fire into their bellies﴾ i.e., filling their bellies,

﴿fire﴾ meaning: they consume what leads to the Fire, so it is as if it were fire. It is narrated that the consumer of orphans' property will be raised on the Day of Resurrection, with smoke coming out from his grave, and from his mouth, his nose, and his ears, so people will recognize that he used to consume the orphan's property in the world.

﴿And they will burn﴾ (وَسَيُصْلَوْنَ, wa-sa-yuṣlawna) is the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir (Shāmī) and Abū Bakr, meaning: they will enter ﴿a blaze﴾ (saʿīran), a fire among the fires, whose description is unspecified.

﴿Allah enjoins upon you﴾ (yuwassikum Allah): He commands you, charges you (ya'hadu ilaykum), and orders you ﴿concerning your children﴾ (fi awladikum), that is, concerning the matter of their inheritance. This is a general statement (ijmal) whose detail follows: ﴿to the male, a portion equal to that of two females﴾. That is, to the male among them, meaning among your children. The word referring back (al-raji') has been omitted because it is understood, as in the saying of the Arabs: "Samn manawan bi-dirham" ("ghee, two manns for a dirham"). He began with the share of the male and did not say "for the two females, a portion equal to the share of the male, or for the female, half the share of the male," because of his superiority, just as his share is doubled for that reason. Also, they used to give inheritance only to males and not to females, and this was the cause of the revelation of the verse. It was said: it is sufficient for the males that the share of the females is doubled for them, so that they would not be excessive in the shares of the females until the females are deprived, despite their connection through kinship in the same manner in which the males are connected. The intended meaning is the case of joint inheritance: when a male and two females are together, the male has two shares, just as the two females have two shares. As for the case of a single heir, a son takes the whole estate, and two daughters take two-thirds. The evidence for this is that He followed it with the ruling for the case of being alone, with His words: ﴿But if they are (p-335) women﴾, that is, if the children are women only, meaning daughters with no son among them, ﴿more than two﴾, where "fawqa" is a second predicate of "kana" (was), or a qualifier of "nisa'" (women), that is, women exceeding two.

﴿For them is two-thirds of what he left﴾, that is, the deceased, because the verse concerns inheritance, so it is known that the one who leaves is the deceased. ﴿And if there is only one, for her is half﴾, that is, if the one born is alone. (Wahida) is read by Madani with the nominative on "kana" as the complete verb (kana al-tammah). The accusative is more suitable to His words: ﴿But if they are women﴾. If you ask: He has mentioned the ruling for two daughters when they are together with a son, and the ruling for daughters and a daughter when alone, but He has not mentioned the ruling for two daughters when alone, so what is their ruling? I say: their ruling is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, placed them in the position of one (daughter), not the position of a group. Others among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, gave them the ruling of a group, in accordance with His words: ﴿to the male, a portion equal to that of two females﴾. This is because whoever dies leaving a daughter and a son, the third is for the daughter and the two-thirds for the son. So when one daughter receives a third, two daughters receive two-thirds. Also, He said at the end of the surah: ﴿If a man dies leaving no child and he has a sister, for her is half of what he left, and he inherits from her if she has no child. But if there are two (sisters), for them is two-thirds of what he left﴾. Two daughters are closer in kinship to the deceased than two sisters, so they assigned to them what Allah assigned to the two sisters, and did not diminish their share below the share of one who is more distant than them. Also, since the daughter, when with her brother, is due a third, it is more fitting that she be due a third when she is with a sister like her, and her sister would have with her the same share that would be due to her also with her brother had she been alone with him; so the two of them are due two-thirds. The verse also indicates that the whole estate belongs to the male if there is no female with him, because He made the male's portion equal to the portion of two females, and He has given the female half when she is alone, so it is known that the male, when alone, has double the half, which is the whole.

The pronoun in ﴿and for his parents﴾ refers to the deceased. The intended meaning is the father and the mother, but the male is given precedence. ﴿For each one of them is a sixth﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "li-abawayhi" (for his parents), by repetition of the governing word. The benefit of this substitution is that if it had been said "and for his parents is a sixth," its apparent meaning would be that they share it. If it had been said "and for his parents are two sixths," it would have suggested dividing the two sixths between them, equally or otherwise. If it had been said "and for each one of his parents is a sixth," the benefit of emphasis would be lost, which is the detail after the general statement. "Al-sudus" (the sixth) is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is "li-abawayhi," and the substitute stands between them for clarification. Al-Hasan read "al-sudsu," "al-rub'u," "al-thumnu," and "al-thuluthu" with the lightened vowel.

﴿From what he left, if he had a child﴾: "walad" applies to the male and the female. ﴿But if he had no child, and his parents inherit from him, then for his mother is a third﴾, that is, of what he left. The meaning is: ﴿and his parents inherit from him﴾ alone, because if his parents inherit from him together with one of the spouses, the mother's share is a third of what remains after the spouse's share is removed, not a third of what he left, because the father is stronger than the mother in inheritance, as evidenced by the fact that he has double her share when they are alone. So if a third were assigned to her in full, that would lead to reducing his share below hers. For if a woman leaves a husband and two parents, the husband takes a half and the mother a third, and the remainder goes to the father; the mother then takes two shares and the father one share, so the ruling reverts to the female having the equivalent of the share of two males. (Fa-li-ummihi) is read with a kasra on the hamza by Hamza and 'Ali, due to the proximity of the kasra of the lam.

﴿But if he has siblings, then for his mother is a sixth﴾: if the deceased has two or more siblings, male and female, then his mother has a sixth. A single brother does not exclude her, and full siblings, half-siblings from the father's side (al-'allat), and half-siblings from the mother's side (al-akhyaf) are equal in excluding the mother.

﴿After a bequest﴾ (min ba'di wasiyyatin) is connected to what precedes it, namely the division of all the inheritances, not only to what immediately follows it. As if it were said: the division of these shares is ﴿after a bequest he bequeaths﴾. "Yusa" (bequeaths) with a fatha on the sad is read by Makki, Shami, Hammad, and Yahya, who agreed with al-A'sha in the first instance, and by Hafs in the second, due to the proximity of "yurathu" (inherited). He read the first with a kasra due to the proximity of ﴿Allah enjoins upon you﴾. The rest read both with kasra on the sad, that is, the deceased bequeaths. ﴿Or a debt.﴾ The difficulty is that the debt takes precedence over the bequest in the Law, whereas the bequest is mentioned before the debt in the recitation. The answer is that "aw" (or) does not indicate order. Do you not see that when you say "Zayd came to me, or 'Amr," the meaning is: one of the two men came to me? So the sense of His words: ﴿after a bequest he bequeaths or a debt﴾ is: after one of these two things, the bequest or the debt. If it had been stated with this wording, order would not be indicated, and it would be permissible to put the later first and the earlier last, as here. We placed the debt before the bequest on the basis of the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "Verily, the debt comes before the bequest." Also, the bequest resembles inheritance in that it is a gift without consideration, so paying it could be burdensome to the heirs, and its fulfilment could be liable to neglect, unlike the debt. So the bequest is mentioned before the debt so that they would hasten to fulfil it along with the debt.

﴿Your fathers and your sons﴾: "aba'ukum" is the subject (mubtada'), "wa-abna'ukum" is conjoined to it, and the predicate is ﴿you do not know﴾. ﴿Which of them﴾ (ayyuhum) is a subject whose predicate is ﴿nearer to you﴾ (aqrabu lakum), and the clause is in the accusative position governed by "tadrun" (you know). ﴿In benefit﴾ (nafan) is a specification (tamyiz). The meaning: Allah prescribed the obligatory shares according to what is wisdom in His knowledge. Had He left that to you, you would not know which of them is more beneficial to you, and you would distribute the wealth without wisdom. The disparity in the portions follows the disparity in benefits, and you do not know its disparity, so Allah undertook that out of His bounty, and did not leave it to your reasoning, because of your inability to know the measures. This clause is a parenthetical emphatic statement (i'tiradiyyah), having no place in the grammatical structure. ﴿An obligation﴾ (fari'atan) is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar), that is: He obligated that as an obligation. ﴿From Allah. Indeed Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of things before their creation, ﴿Wise﴾ in all that He has obligated and apportioned of inheritances and other matters.

[p-338] **"And for you is half of what your wives leave, if they have no child."** That is, your wives. **"If they have no child"**, meaning no son or daughter.

**"But if they have a child"**, whether from you or from others,

**"then for you is a quarter of what they leave, after any bequest they make or debt. And for them is a quarter of what you leave if you have no child; but if you have a child, then for them is an eighth of what you leave, after any bequest you make or debt."** The single wife and the plural wives are equal in the quarter and the eighth. He made the husband's share double the wife's share, as indicated by His saying: **"To the male a portion equal to that of two females."**

**"And if a man"**, meaning the deceased, who is the subject of *kāna* (was). **"Leaves an inheritance (yūrathu)"** comes from *wuritha*, meaning that an inheritance is left by him, and this is a description of *rajul* (man). **"Kalāla"** is the predicate of *kāna*, meaning: if a man is one whose estate is inherited as *kalāla*. Alternatively, *yūrathu* is the predicate of *kāna*, and *kalāla* is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in *yūrathu*. *Al-kalāla* is applied to one who leaves neither a child nor a parent, and also to one who is neither a child nor a parent of the deceased. Originally it is a verbal noun meaning *al-kalāl*, which is the loss of strength due to fatigue.

**"Or a woman"** is coordinated with *rajul* (man). **"And he has a brother or a sister"**, that is, a maternal sibling. If you say: the man and the woman have already been mentioned, so why is the pronoun singular and masculine? I say: its singularity is because *aw* (or) is for one of two things. Its masculinity is because it refers to *rajul*, since it is masculine and mentioned first; or it refers to one of the two, and that is masculine.

**"Then each one of them receives a sixth. But if they are more than that"**, more than one, **"then they are partners in the third"**, because they are entitled through maternal kinship, and that does not inherit more than a third. For this reason the male among them is not preferred over the female. **"After any bequest that is made or debt."** The bequest is repeated because the testators differ. The first is the parents and children; the second is the wife; the third is the husband; the fourth is the *kalāla*.

**"Not causing harm."** This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that he makes the bequest while not harming his heirs. That is, by **"a bequest from Allah"**, which is a verbal noun for emphasis, meaning: He enjoins you thus, as a bequest. **"And Allah is All-Knowing"** of whoever deviates or is just in his bequest,

**"Forbearing"** toward the wrongdoer, not hastening to punish him. This is a warning. If you say: where is the circumstantial subject (*dhū al-ḥāl*) for the one who reads *yūṣā bihā* (is bequeathed)? I say: *yūṣī* (he bequeaths) is understood to be implied and accusative as the agent, because when it was said *yūṣā bihā* (it is bequeathed), it was known that there is a testator. Just as *rijāl* (men) is the agent of what indicates it: *yusabbiḥu* (glorify), because when it was said **"He is glorified for Him"** [24:36], it was known that there is one who glorifies, so *yusabbiḥu* is understood.

[p-339] Know that the heirs are of categories. The first are the *aṣḥāb al-farāʾiḍ* (holders of fixed shares), who are those for whom there are determined portions. For example: the daughter, who receives a half, and two-thirds for two or more. The daughter of a son, however low her descent, is, in the absence of children, like the daughter; and she receives a sixth alongside the daughter of the loins (*ṣulbiyya*). She is excluded by a son or two daughters of the loins, except if there is a boy with her, in which case he makes her a residuary (*yaʿṣibuhā*). The full sisters and the consanguine sisters: they, in the absence of a child or a son's child, are like the daughters. The paternal sisters, in the absence of full sisters, are like the full sisters. The two groups become residuaries alongside a daughter or a daughter of a son. They are excluded by a son, a son's son however low, a father, a grandfather according to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), and a maternal sibling. For one of them there is a sixth, and for two or more there is a third. Their males are like their females. They are excluded by a child, a son's child however low, a father, or a grandfather.

The father: he has a sixth alongside a son or a son's son however low, and alongside a daughter or a daughter of a son however low he has a sixth plus the remainder. The grandfather: he is the father's father, and in the absence of the father he is like the father, except in reducing the mother to a third of what remains. The mother: she has a sixth alongside a child or a son's child however low, or alongside two or more of the siblings of any kind. She has a third of the whole in the absence of these, and a third of what remains after the fixed share of one of the spouses in the case of a husband with parents, or a wife with parents. The grandmother: she has a sixth, however many there are, whether maternal or paternal. The more distant is excluded by the nearer. All are excluded by the mother, and the paternal grandmothers by the father. The husband: he has a quarter alongside a child or a son's child however low, and in the absence of these, a half. The wife: she has an eighth alongside a child or a son's child however low, and in the absence of these, a quarter.

The residuaries (*ʿaṣaba*): they are those who inherit what remains of the fixed shares. The first of them is the son, then his son however low, then the father, then his father however high, then the full brother, then the consanguine brother, then the son of the full brother, then the son of the consanguine brother, then the paternal uncles, then the uncles of the father, then the uncles of the grandfather, then the manumitter, then his residuaries in order. Those whose fixed share is a half or two-thirds become residuaries through their sisters, not otherwise. The distant kin (*dhawū al-arḥām*): they are the relatives who are neither residuaries nor holders of fixed shares, and their order is like the order of the residuaries.

"That" is a reference to the rulings mentioned in the sections on orphans, bequests, and inheritances.

"The limits of Allah" (ḥudūd Allāh): He called them "limits" (ḥudūd) because the laws are like the boundaries (ḥudūd, sing. ḥadd) set down for those who are legally responsible, and it is not permissible for them to transgress them.

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾

The Qur'anic quotations are rendered in the same ﴿ ﴾ markers, and the Arabic words under grammatical discussion are kept in Arabic script.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 14:

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger and transgresses His limits, He will admit him to a Fire, abiding therein.﴾ The word انتصب (intasaba, "was put in the accusative") and خالِدِينَ وخالِدًا (khalidin wa khalidan, "abiding" in two forms) are in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, "in the state of abiding"). It was pluralized once and singularized another time, in consideration of the meaning of مَن (man, "whoever") and of its wording. نُدْخِلْهُ (nudkhilhu, "We will admit him") in both places is read by Madani and Shami (the Medinan and Syrian readers).

﴿And for him is a humiliating punishment﴾, because of his humiliation before Allah. The Mu'tazila (a theological school that held that the grave sinner is in an intermediate position) and the Khawarij (a early sect that declared the grave sinner a disbeliever) have no basis in this verse, for it concerns the disbelievers. The disbeliever is the one who transgresses all the limits, whereas the believing sinner is obedient through his faith and does not transgress the boundary of tawhid (the affirmation of Allah's oneness). For this reason al-Ḍaḥḥāk interpreted the disobedience here as shirk (associating partners with Allah). Al-Kalbi said: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ by his disbelief in dividing the inheritances, ﴿and transgresses His limits﴾ by considering them lawful.

Then He addressed the rulers and said: ﴿And those who﴾ (wa-allatī) is the plural of allatī, and its place in the i'rab is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada').

﴿come to commit lewdness﴾, i.e., fornication (al-zina), because of its greater ugliness above many other vile deeds. It is said: atā al-fāḥisha, wa-jā'ahā, wa-rahiqahā, wa-ghashiyahā, all with the same meaning.

﴿of your women﴾: min is for partitive (li-l-tab'īḍ). The predicate (khabar) is ﴿then seek testimony against them﴾, i.e., request the testimony.

﴿four of you﴾, from among the believers. ﴿If they testify﴾ to the fornication, ﴿then confine them to the houses﴾, i.e., imprison them, ﴿until death takes them﴾, i.e., the angels of death, like His saying: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ [al-Nahl: 28]. Or: until death takes them and claims their souls.

﴿Or God makes for them﴾: it is said that "aw" here means "illā an" (except that).

﴿a way﴾, other than this. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both: "The way for the virgin is a hundred lashes and exile for a year, and for the married (thayyib) it is stoning," based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): « "Take from me, take from me! God has made for them a way: the virgin with the virgin, a hundred lashes and exile for a year; and the married with the married, a hundred lashes and stoning with stones." »

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 16:**

﴿And the two who commit it﴾: he means the male fornicator and the female fornicator. Reading ﴿وَاللَّذَانِ﴾ with a doubled nūn (*al-lazzāni*) is attributed to Makkī (Ibn Kathīr).

﴿who commit it among you﴾: that is, the indecency (al-fāḥisha).

﴿Then cause them hurt﴾ by rebuke and reproach, and say to them: "Are you not ashamed? Do you not fear God?" ﴿But if they repent﴾ from the indecency ﴿and amend﴾ and change their condition, ﴿then leave them alone﴾: cut off the rebuke and blame. ﴿Indeed, God is ever Relenting, Merciful﴾: He accepts the repentance of the penitent and has mercy upon him.

Al-Ḥasan said: The first thing revealed regarding the prescribed punishment for fornication was harm (al-adhā), then imprisonment (al-ḥabs), then flogging (al-jald) or stoning (al-rajm). So the order of revelation was contrary to the order of recitation.

The conclusion is: if both of them are muḥṣan (married and free, i.e., eligible for the full penalty), their punishment is stoning (al-rajm) alone. If both are non-muḥṣan, their punishment is flogging (al-jald) alone. If one of them is muḥṣan and the other is not, then the muḥṣan one receives stoning and the other receives flogging.

Ibn Baḥr said: The first verse concerns female homosexuals (al-saḥḥāqāt), the second concerns male homosexuals (al-lawwāṭīn), and the one in Surat al-Nūr concerns the male fornicator and the female fornicator. This is a clear proof for Abū Ḥanīfa, may God have mercy on him, that one who commits sodomy (al-liwāṭa) is disciplined (yu'azzaru) and is not subject to the prescribed punishment (lā yuḥaddu).

Mujāhid said: the verse of harm concerns sodomy (al-liwāṭa).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 17:

﴿Repentance is only [accepted] from Allah for those who do wrong out of ignorance⦆ ... 

Let me correct that and translate the passage fully:

"Repentance [accepted by Allah]" is only for the one whom Allah accepts in repentance when He accepts his repentance. That is, its acceptance is only ﴿upon Allah﴾, and by this is not meant obligation, since nothing is obligatory upon Allah. Rather, it is an emphasis of the promise, meaning that it will certainly occur, like an obligation that is not abandoned.

﴿For those who do evil⦆ — the sin — because of the evil of its punishment, ﴿out of ignorance﴾ (in a position of circumstantial state): that is, they do evil being ignorant and foolish, because committing an ugly deed is something that folly calls for. And from Mujahid: whoever disobeys Allah is ignorant until he desists from his ignorance. It was also said: their ignorance is their choosing the fleeting pleasure over the enduring one. It was also said: they did not ignore that it was a sin, but they were ignorant of the reality of its punishment. ﴿Then they repent soon﴾, from a near time, which is what comes before the presence of death. Do you not see His saying: ﴿until, when death comes to one of them﴾? So He made clear that the time of the death-throes is the time in which repentance is not accepted. From al-Dahhak: every repentance before death is "soon." From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: before he looks upon the Angel of Death. And from him (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah, the Exalted, accepts the repentance of the servant so long as he has not begun to gasp (in death-rattle)." The "min" here is partitive, meaning they repent within part of a near time, as if He called the interval between the occurrence of the disobedience and the presence of death a "near time."

﴿Then those — Allah will accept repentance from them﴾: a promise that this will be fulfilled, and an announcement that forgiveness will certainly occur.

﴿And Allah is ever Knowing⦆ of their resolve to repent ﴿Wise⦆, who ruled that regret is repentance.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 18:

﴿And repentance is not for those who do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have repented now."﴾ That is: there is no repentance for those who commit sins and postpone their repentance until the state of obligation (taklif) ceases, by the presence of the signs of death and the witnessing of the Angel of Death (Malak al-Mawt). Indeed, the repentance of these people is not accepted, because it is a state of compulsion (idtirar), not a state of choice (ikhtiyar), and the acceptance of repentance is a reward, and no promise of it is given except to one who chooses. ﴿Nor for those who die﴾ — in a position of genitive by coordination (ʿatf) with ﴿those who do evil deeds﴾; that is: repentance is not for those who do evil deeds, nor for those who die ﴿while they are disbelievers﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the first verse concerns the believers, the middle one concerns the hypocrites, and the last concerns the disbelievers. In some copies of the Qur'an there is "la" with two lams (lā'īn), and it is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is: ﴿for them We have prepared a painful punishment﴾. That is: We have readied (hayya'na) from al-ʿatīd, which means "the ready/present," or the original form is a'dadna, and the dal was changed into a ta'.

(p-343)

The man would inherit his deceased relative's wife by throwing his garment over her, and then he would marry her without a dower (mahr). So this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. That is, to take them by way of inheritance, as inherited property is taken, while they are unwilling to that, or are compelled (*karhan*). With the vowel *fatha* (*karhan*) it derives from *al-karahah* (aversion); with *damma* (*kurhan*), Hamza and Ali read it, deriving from *al-ikrah* (compulsion). It is a verbal noun (*masdar*) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the object. Restricting the prohibition to aversion does not imply permission when aversion is absent, because specifying a thing by mention does not imply the negation of what is other than it, as in His words: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra' 31], and ﴿nor restrain them﴾.

It was the custom that when a man married a woman whom he did not desire, he would keep her in confinement, treating her badly, so that she would ransom herself from him with her property and seek release (*khul'*). So it was said: ﴿nor restrain them﴾. It is in the accusative (*mansub*) by coordination (*'atf*) with ﴿to inherit﴾, and "lā" is for emphasizing the negation. That is: it is not lawful for you to inherit women, nor to restrain them. Or it is in the jussive (*majzum*) by a prohibition in a new sentence (*isti'naf*), in which case it is permissible to pause at ﴿karhan﴾. *Al-'adl* means confinement and constriction.

﴿that you may take away part of what you have given them﴾ of the dower; the *lam* is connected to "restrain" (*ta'ḍulū*). ﴿unless they commit a flagrant immorality﴾, which is disobedience (*nushuz*) and harming the husband and his family with abuse. That is: unless the bad treatment comes from their side, in which case you are excused for seeking *khul'*. It is reported from al-Hasan that the immorality is fornication (*zina*), and if she commits it, it becomes lawful for her husband to ask her for *khul'*. ﴿mubayyinah﴾ (clearly evident) with a *fatha* on the *ya'* is read by Makki and Abu Bakr. The exception is from a more general category of the adverbial of time or of the object of purpose, as if it were said: "nor restrain them at any time, except the time when they commit a flagrant immorality," or: "nor restrain them for any cause, except that they commit a flagrant immorality."

They used to treat women badly in companionship, so it was said to them: ﴿and live with them in kindness﴾, which is equity in staying the night, in maintenance, and in gentleness of speech.

﴿Then if you dislike them﴾ because of their ugliness, or the badness of their character.

﴿then it may be that you dislike a thing and Allah places in it﴾ in that thing, or in the aversion itself,

﴿much good﴾: abundant wealth, or a righteous child. The meaning is: if you dislike them, do not separate from them merely because of the aversion of the self alone, for the self may dislike what is more beneficial in (p-٣٤٤) religion and more conducive to good, and love what is its opposite. Rather, consider the causes of righteousness. His words ﴿then it may be that you dislike﴾ are correct as a response to the condition, because the meaning is: "If you dislike them, then be patient with them despite the aversion, for perhaps in what you dislike there is much good that is not in what you love."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 20:

It was the custom that when a man saw a woman and was attracted to her, he would slander the wife he had (bahata allati tahtahu) and accuse her of immorality, until he forced her to ransom herself from him with what he had given her. So it was said: ﴿And if you desire to exchange one spouse for another﴾, that is, to divorce one woman and marry another,

﴿and you have given one of them﴾, and you have given one of the wives, so the word "spouse" here is meant in the plural, because the address is to a group of men,

﴿a great amount﴾ (qintaran), meaning a vast amount of wealth, as has passed in Al ʿImran. ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said from the pulpit: "Do not exaggerate in the bridal gifts of women." A woman said: "Shall we follow your words or the words of Allah: ﴿and you have given one of them a great amount﴾?" ʿUmar said: "Every person knows more than ʿUmar. Marry on whatever terms you wish." ﴿Then take not from it﴾ (from the qintar) ﴿anything. Would you take it by slander and manifest sin?﴾, that is, clear. Buhtan (slander) means that you confront a man with an ugly matter, accusing him of it while he is innocent of it, because he is thereby stunned (yubhat), that is, bewildered. Buhtanan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: stunned and sinning.

Then He denounced taking the bridal gift (mahr) after intimacy (ifda'), saying: ﴿And how could you take it, when you have gone in unto one another?﴾ That is, they were alone together without any barrier; from the same root comes al-fada' (open space). The verse is evidence for us that valid seclusion (al-khalwah al-sahihah) confirms the mahr, since He denounced taking it and gave as the reason ﴿and they have taken from you a solemn covenant﴾, that is, a firm pledge. This is the saying of God Most High: ﴿Then either retain them in kindness or release them with good treatment﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229]. God Most High imposed this covenant on His servants for the sake of women, so it is like their taking it; or it is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him (p-345): "Be good to women, for they are prisoners in your hands. You have taken them under the trust of God, and made their private parts lawful to you by the word of God."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 22:

When the verse ﴿It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ was revealed, they said: "We leave this practice. We do not inherit them against their will, but we propose to them and marry them with their consent." So it was said to them: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾. It was also said that the intended meaning of "nikah" (marriage) here is "wat'" (sexual intercourse), i.e., do not have intercourse with those with whom your fathers had intercourse. In this is the prohibition of having intercourse with the one whom one's father had intercourse with, whether by marriage, by right of ownership (milk al-yamin), or by fornication (zina), as is our school's position, and this is the view of many of the exegetes (mufassirun). When they said: "We used to do that; what is the status of what was done by us?" He said: ﴿except what has already passed﴾, meaning: but what has already passed, for you will not be held accountable for it. The exception is disjunctive (munqati'), according to Sibawayh. Then he explained the nature of this contract in the present, saying: ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination﴾, extremely ugly, ﴿and hateful﴾ and detested in the sight of Allah and in the sight of the believers. Some of their men who had honor and dignity used to despise it, and they called it "the marriage of hatred" (nikah al-maqt), and the child born from it was called "al-maqti" (the one of hatred). ﴿And evil is the way﴾, meaning: what an evil way that is.

When he had mentioned at the beginning of the surah the marriage of **﴿what is lawful (ما طاب)﴾**, meaning what is permitted, **﴿from women﴾**, and had mentioned some of what he had forbidden before this, namely the wives of fathers, he then mentioned the remaining forbidden women. They are seven by blood relation and seven by means of a cause. He began with blood relation and said: **﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾**. What is meant is the prohibition of marrying them, according to some scholars. We have set out the preferred view in *Sharh al-Manar* (an explanatory commentary on the legal manual *al-Manar*). The grandmother, whether on the mother's or the father's side, is included among them. **﴿And your daughters﴾**: the daughters of a son and the daughters of a daughter are included among them. The principle is that when a plural is set against a plural, the individuals are distributed over the individuals, so that each man is forbidden his own mother and his own daughter. (p-٣٤٦) **﴿And your sisters﴾**, whether full sisters, or sisters through the father only, or through the mother only.

**﴿And your paternal aunts﴾**, in all three of those senses.

**﴿And your maternal aunts﴾**, likewise.

**﴿And your brother's daughters﴾**, likewise.

**﴿And your sister's daughters﴾**, likewise.

Then he turned to the causes, saying: **﴿And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through nursing﴾**. God, exalted is He, placed nursing in the position of blood kinship. Thus He called the woman who nurses an infant the infant's mother, and the nursling a sister. Likewise, the husband of the nursing woman is the infant's father, her parents are his grandparents, and her sister is his paternal aunt. Every child born to him from someone other than the nursing woman, whether before or after the nursing, is his brother or sister on the father's side. The mother of the nursing woman is his grandmother, and her sister is his maternal aunt. Every child born to her from this husband is his brother or sister on both the father's and mother's side. Every child born to her from another man is his brother or sister on the mother's side. The basis for this is his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: "What is forbidden by blood is forbidden by nursing." **﴿And the mothers of your wives﴾**: they are forbidden by the contract alone. **﴿And your stepdaughters (rabā'ib)﴾**: the child of a woman by a former husband is called *rabīb* (masculine) or *rabība* (feminine), because he or she is raised (*yarubbuhumā*) by the stepfather in the same way as he raises his own child in most cases. The term was then extended, so that they were called by this name even if he did not raise them. **﴿Who are in your guardianship (fī ḥujūrikum)﴾**. Dawud said: if she is not under his guardianship, she is not forbidden. We reply: the mention of the guardianship describes the usual situation and is not a condition. Its purpose is to give the reason for the prohibition, namely that they are in your care, or that they are about to be in your care. It is as though, in contracting marriage to their mothers, you were contracting marriage to your own daughters.

**﴿Of your wives with whom you have consummated (the marriage)﴾**. This phrase is connected to *rabā'ibikum*. That is, a stepdaughter of a woman with whom the man has consummated the marriage is forbidden to him, while she is lawful to him if he has not consummated the marriage with her mother. "Consummation" (*dukhūl*) is a metaphor for sexual intercourse, as in their saying *banā 'alayhā* (he built upon her) and *ḍaraba 'alayhā al-ḥijāb* (he drew the veil over her), meaning you brought them behind the curtain. The particle *bi* here marks transitivity. Touching and similar acts take the place of consummation. Some scholars have treated the phrase *allatī dakhaltum bihinna* as a qualifying description of both the earlier and the later women. This is not correct, because a single qualifier cannot apply to two nouns governed by different operators. The first word *nisā'ikum* is in the genitive by annexation, while the second is governed by *min*. You cannot say *marartu bi-nisā'ika* (I passed by your women) and *harabtu min nisā'i Zaydin al-ẓarīfāt* (I fled from the charming women of Zayd), with the word *al-ẓarīfāt* being an adjective describing these women. This is what al-Zajjaj and others have said. This view is preferable to what the author of *al-Kashshāf* said on this point. **﴿But if you have not consummated (the marriage) with them, there is no blame upon you﴾**: there is no sin on you in marrying their daughters if you have separated from their mothers, or if the mothers have died.

**﴿And the wives of your sons﴾**: this is the plural of *ḥalīla*, which means a wife, because each of the spouses is lawful to the other (*yaḥillu*), or because each lies in the bed of the other (*yaḥillu firāsh al-ākhar*). It derives either from *ḥill* (lawfulness) or from *ḥulūl* (lodging).

**﴿Those who are from your loins﴾**: this excludes those whom you have adopted. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) married Zaynab after Zayd had divorced her, and God, exalted is He, said: **﴿So that there may be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾** (Al-Ahzab 33:37). This clause does not mean that the wife of a son by nursing is lawful.

**﴿And that you should combine two sisters﴾**: that is, in marriage. This phrase is in the nominative position, coordinated with the forbidden women. That is, it is forbidden to you to combine two sisters.

**﴿Except what has already passed﴾**: but what has passed is forgiven, as is shown by His saying: **﴿Indeed, God is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾**.

It is related from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him, that the people of the time of ignorance (*jāhiliyya*) recognised all these prohibitions except marrying the wife of a father and combining two sisters. For this reason He said regarding these two: **﴿except what has already passed﴾**.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 24:

﴿And [forbidden to you are] the married women (al-muhsanat) among women,﴾ that is, those who have husbands, because they have guarded their chastity (ihsan) through marriage. al-Kisa'i read the vowel of the ṣād (ṣād) here as fatḥa (fatha), and throughout the rest of the Qur'an as kasra (kasra). Others read it with fatḥa throughout the entire Qur'an.

﴿except what your right hands possess﴾ through captivity (saby), when her husband is in the abode of war. The meaning is: marriage to women who are already married is forbidden to you, that is, those who have husbands, except those you have acquired by capture and removal from their husbands. The separation occurs through the difference of the two abodes, not through the capture itself. Thus the spoils become lawful by ownership of the right hand after istibra' (the waiting period to establish that a woman is not pregnant) ﴿the decree of God upon you﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar): God has prescribed that upon you as a prescription (kitaban), and has made it an obligation (fari'a), namely the prohibition of what He has prohibited. ﴿And lawful to you﴾ is conjoined to the implied verb that governs "the decree of God": God has decreed upon you the prohibition of that, ﴿and lawful to you﴾ ﴿is what lies beyond these﴾, that is, whatever is other than the aforementioned prohibited persons. (wa-uhilla) is read by the Kufans, except Abu Bakr, as a conjunction with (ḥurrimat).

﴿that you seek﴾ is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu): He has made clear to you what is lawful from what is forbidden, so that you may seek, or it is a substitute for ﴿what lies beyond these﴾. The object of "you seek" is implied, and it is the women; the better view is not to imply it.

﴿with your wealth﴾ means the bridal gifts (mahr). In this there is evidence that marriage cannot occur except with a bridal gift, that it is obligatory even if not specified, that something other than property is not suitable as a bridal gift, and that a small amount is not suitable as a bridal gift, since a single grain is not ordinarily considered property.

﴿chaste (muhsinin)﴾ in the state of being those who guard their chastity.

﴿not fornicating (musafihin)﴾ so that you do not waste your wealth and impoverish yourselves in what is not lawful for you, thereby losing your religion and your worldly life. There is no greater corruption than combining the two losses. Ihsan means chastity and guarding oneself from falling into what is unlawful. The musafih is the fornicator, from safh, which is the pouring out of semen.

﴿So for whatever you have enjoyed from them﴾ "ma" refers to what you have married from among them. ﴿give them their wages (ujur)﴾, that is, their bridal gifts, because the bridal gift is a reward for the sexual union. Thus "ma" carries the meaning of women. "Min" is partitive or explanatory. The pronoun returns to it according to the wording in "bihi" and according to the meaning in "fa-atuhunna." ﴿as an obligation (fariḍa)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "wages": that is, prescribed; or it is placed in the position of giving (iitaʾ), because giving is prescribed; or it is an emphatic verbal noun: He prescribed that as a prescription.

﴿And there is no blame upon you regarding what you agree upon after the obligation﴾ regarding what she remits of the bridal gift, or what she gives up of all of it, or what he adds to it beyond its amount, or regarding what the two agree upon of continuing the marriage or separation.

﴿Indeed, God is ever Knowing﴾ of things before their creation, ﴿Wise﴾ regarding what He has prescribed for them of the contract of marriage, by which lineages are preserved. (p-349) It is said that His saying ﴿So for whatever you have enjoyed﴾ was revealed concerning temporary marriage (mut'a), which was for three days when God granted Makkah to His Messenger, and then it was abrogated (nusikhat).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 25:

﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [to marry] free believing women﴾ (ṭawl): bounty and surplus. It is said: "So-and-so has ṭawl over me," meaning he has bounty and excess. It is the object of "cannot afford" (yastaṭiʿ).

﴿to marry﴾ (an yankiḥa) is the object of ṭawl, since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) and so governs like its verb. Alternatively, it is a substitute (badal) for "ṭawl."

﴿free believing women﴾ (al-muḥṣanāt al-muʾmināt): free Muslim women.

﴿then [let him marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing maidens﴾: that is, let him marry a slave woman from the Muslim female slaves. His saying "from your maidens" means: from the maidens of the Muslims. The meaning is: whoever cannot afford additional wealth and ample means by which to reach marriage with a free woman, let him marry a slave woman. Marrying a slave woman who is a People of the Book (kitābiyya) is permissible according to us. The restriction in the text is for recommendation (istiḥbāb), as evidenced by the fact that faith is not a condition for free women by consensus, even though it is stipulated here. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Among the things God has made easy for this community is marrying a slave woman, a Jewish woman, or a Christian woman, even if one is wealthy." There is evidence in this for us in the matter of ṭawl.

﴿And God knows best your faith﴾: this contains an indication of accepting the apparent faith of these women, and evidence that faith is assent (taṣdīq) without the action of the tongue, because knowledge of faith as heard does not differ. ﴿Some of you are from others﴾: that is, do not disdain marrying slave women, for all of you are children of Adam. This is a warning against reproaching others over lineage and boasting about noble descent.

﴿So marry them with the permission of their people﴾ (ahlihinna): their masters. This is a proof for us that they may conduct the contract themselves, because He required the permission of the masters, not their contracting. And it is not permitted for a male or female slave to marry except with the permission of the master.

﴿And give them their wages (ujūrahunna) in accordance with what is reasonable﴾: pay to them their dowries (muhūrahunna) without delay or harm. The owners of their dowries are their masters, so paying them is paying the masters, since they and what is in their hands are the property of the masters. Or the meaning is: "and give to their masters," with the word "masters" omitted.

﴿chaste (muḥṣanāt)﴾: modest, a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object in "give them."

﴿not fornicators (musāfiḥāt)﴾: openly unchaste. ﴿nor taking lovers in secret (akhdān)﴾: secretly unchaste. And al-akhdān are secret friends.

﴿And when they are chaste (uḥṣinna)﴾ by marriage. The Kufan reader, other than Ḥafṣ, reads "aḥṣanna."

﴿And if they commit a gross indecency (fāḥisha)﴾: adultery (zinā), ﴿then upon them is half of the punishment for free women (al-muḥṣanāt)﴾: that is, free women.

﴿of the chastisement﴾: of the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), meaning fifty lashes. His saying "half of what is for free women" indicates that it is flogging, not stoning, since stoning cannot be halved. And "free women" here means free women who have not been married.

﴿That﴾: that is, marrying slave women is ﴿for him among you who fears sin (ʿanat)﴾: for him who fears the sin to which overpowering desire leads. The root meaning of ʿanat is the breaking of a bone after it has been set, so it is used metaphorically for every hardship and harm, and there is no harm greater than committing sins. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: it is adultery, because it is the cause of ruin.

﴿And that you be patient﴾ is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtadaʾ): that is, your restraint from marrying slave women while remaining chaste.

﴿is better for you﴾, because in it there is the enslavement of offspring, and because she is one who goes out often, enters often, is degraded and humiliated. All of this is deficiency that returns to the one who marries her, and abasement. Honor is among the attributes of the believers. And in a hadith: "Free women are the well-being of the house, and slave women are the ruin of the house."

﴿And God is Forgiving﴾: He covers what is forbidden. ﴿Merciful﴾: He removes what is forbidden.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 26:

﴿Allah wishes to make [it] clear to you﴾. Its original form is: "Allah wishes that He make clear to you," so the lam (al-lam, the particle of purpose/emphasis) was added to emphasize the wish for clarification, just as it is added in "lā abā laka" (may you have no father), to emphasize the attribution of the father. The meaning is: Allah wishes to make clear to you what is hidden from you of your welfare and of your most excellent deeds.

﴿And to guide you to the ways (sunan) of those before you﴾. And that He guide you to the paths (manahij) of those who were before you among the prophets and the righteous, and to the ways (turuq) they followed in their religion, so that you may follow them.

﴿And to turn to you [in forgiveness]﴾. That is, He enables you to repent from what you were upon of opposition (al-khilaf). ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ (p-351) of the welfare of His servants, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He has legislated for them.

God desires to turn [in forgiveness] toward you (Allah yurīdu an yatūba ʿalaykum). The repetition serves emphasis, confirmation, and contrast. "And [the others] desire" — the wicked ones.

"Those who follow the passions (al-shahawat) desire that you deviate with a tremendous deviation." This is the deviation from the path of moderation (al-qasd) and truth, and there is no deviation greater than it, through their assisting and agreeing with them in following the passions. It is said: they are the Jews, because they permitted [marriage to] paternal sisters, daughters of a brother, and daughters of a sister. When Allah prohibited these, they said: "Indeed you permit the daughter of your maternal aunt and of your paternal aunt, while your maternal aunt and paternal aunt are forbidden to you, so marry the daughters of the sister and of the brother." Then [this verse] was revealed. He says: they desire that you become fornicators like themselves.

Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you (﴿Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you﴾) by permitting marriage to a slave woman and other concessions.

﴿And man was created weak﴾: he cannot restrain himself from desires, nor bear the hardships of acts of worship.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 29:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾ by what the Sharia has not permitted, such as theft, embezzlement, usurpation, gambling, and contracts of riba (usury).

﴿Except that it be a transaction﴾ meaning, except that a trade occurs. (تِجارَةً) is read by the Kufans (as an accusative after the verb "takūna"). That is: ﴿except that it be﴾ trade ﴿by mutual consent among you﴾, the phrase "by mutual consent" being a qualifier of "transaction." That is: a trade proceeding from mutual consent, by contract or by mutual exchange (al-ta'āṭī). The exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), its meaning being: "But aim for trade that is by mutual consent," or "But trade that is by mutual consent is not prohibited." He singled out trade for mention because most of the means of livelihood are connected to it. The verse indicates the permissibility of sale by mutual exchange (bay' bil-ta'āṭī), the permissibility of a suspended sale (bay' al-mawqūf) when ratification is obtained, since consent is present, and the negation of the option of the meeting (khiyār al-majlis), because it permits consuming wealth through trade by mutual consent without (p-352) restricting it to separation from the place of the contract, and restricting it to that would be an addition to the text.

﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ meaning, whoever is of your kind among the believers, since the believers are like a single soul; or, a man should not kill himself as some ignorant people do; or, the meaning of killing is consuming wealth unjustly, for one who wrongs others is like one who destroys himself; or, do not follow their desires so that you destroy them; or, do not commit what necessitates killing.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ and out of His mercy toward you He alerted you to what preserves your wealth and the continuation of your bodies. It was also said: its meaning is that He commanded the Children of Israel to kill themselves so that it would be a repentance for them and an expiation of their sins; and ﴿to you﴾, O community of Muhammad, ﴿Merciful﴾, in that He did not impose upon you those difficult obligations.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 30:

﴿And whoever does that﴾, i.e., the killing, that is, whoever undertakes to kill souls,

﴿out of enmity and injustice﴾, not by mistake and not by way of retribution (qisas). These two are verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal) or as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu).

﴿then We will drive him into the Fire﴾, We will cause him to enter a particular Fire, severe in punishment. ﴿And that is ever for Allah easy﴾, i.e., his being made to burn in the Fire, ﴿easy﴾, simple. And this threat, with regard to one who deems it lawful (al-mustahill), concerns eternal abiding (al-takhlid); with regard to others, it serves to show that he deserves to enter the Fire, together with Allah's promise of forgiveness for him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 31:

﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove from you your bad deeds﴾. From Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The major sins (kaba'ir) are everything Allah has forbidden from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to His words: ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden﴾." And from him also: "The major sins are three: associating partners with Allah, despairing of the mercy of Allah, and feeling secure from the plan of Allah." It has also been said: what is meant is types of disbelief (kufr), based on the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): (kabira ma tunhawna 'anhu) ("the great [sin] you are forbidden"), and this is disbelief.

﴿And We will cause you to enter an honourable entrance﴾. (madkhalan) is read by Madani (a reader of the Qur'an, i.e. Abu Ja'far/Nafi' school as transmitted from Madina). Both forms carry the sense of a place and of a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿Kariman﴾: good. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Eight verses in Surat al-Nisa' are better for this Ummah than everything the sun rises upon and sets over: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], ﴿And Allah desires to accept your repentance﴾ [al-Nisa': 27], ﴿Allah desires to lighten for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 28], ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove from you﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 110], ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment?﴾ [al-Nisa': 147]."

The Mu'tazila relied on this verse to argue that minor sins are necessarily forgiven upon avoiding major sins, and that major sins are not forgiven. This is invalid, because major and minor sins are equal in relation to His will (mashi'ah), exalted is He: if He wills, He punishes for them, and if He wills, He pardons them, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. So He promised forgiveness for what is below shirk and tied it to His will, exalted is He. And His words: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾ [Hud: 114]. This verse indicates that both minor and major sins may be removed by good deeds, because the word "bad deeds" (sayyi'at) applies to both of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 32:

When the taking of another's wealth without right, and the killing of a soul without just cause, arose from coveting another's wealth and standing, He forbade them from coveting that with which Allah has favoured some people over others in terms of standing and wealth, by saying: ﴿And do not covet that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others.﴾ This is because that favouring is a distribution from Allah, issuing from wisdom, management, and knowledge of the circumstances of the servants, and of what befits everyone whose provision is expanded or restricted. So each one must be content with what has been apportioned to him, and must not envy his brother for his share. Envy (hasad) is that one wishes that thing were his, and that it would leave its owner. Ghibta (emulation) is that one wishes for something like what another has; this is permitted, while the former is forbidden. When the men said, "We hope that our reward will be double the reward of the women," and the women said, "Our burden will be half the burden of the men," as with inheritance, the verse was revealed: ﴿For men there is a share of what they have earned, and for women there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ That is, it is not according to the measure of inheritance.

﴿And ask Allah of His bounty.﴾ For His treasuries never run out. And do not covet what people have of bounty.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing.﴾ So the favouring comes from Him with knowledge of the places of deservingness. Ibn ʿUyayna said: "He did not command asking except in order to give."

(p-354) In a hadith: "Whoever does not ask Allah of His bounty, He becomes angry with him." And in it: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, withholds much good from His servant, and says: I will not give My servant until he asks Me." (And "wa-saluu") is read by Makki and ʿAli.

﴿وَلِكُلٍّ﴾: the genitive complement (al-muḍāf ilayhi) is omitted. Its estimated form is "and for every person" or "for every property."

﴿جَعَلْنا مَوالِيَ﴾ means heirs (wurrāth) who take charge of it and guard it. ﴿مِمّا تَرَكَ الوالِدانِ والأقْرَبُونَ﴾ means "from what the parents and the relatives leave behind." It is a qualifier (ṣifa) of an omitted noun, māl (property), meaning "for every property that the parents have left behind."
