Then He urged forgiveness, and that no one should publicly speak evil of anyone, even by way of retaliation, after having permitted public speech of it, as an exhortation to what is better. He mentioned the showing of good and the concealing of it as a means toward forgiveness, and said: ﴿If you show good﴾ in place of publicly speaking evil ﴿or conceal it﴾ by doing it secretly. Then He joined forgiveness with these two, saying:

﴿Or you forgive an evil﴾, meaning: you erase it from your hearts. The evidence that forgiveness is the intended meaning in mentioning the showing and concealing of good is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Pardoning, Competent﴾, meaning: He has never ceased to be Pardoning of sins, while being Able to exact retribution. So it is incumbent upon you to emulate His way (sunnah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 150:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers, and want to make distinction between Allah and His messengers, and say, "We believe in some and disbelieve in others,"﴾ like the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, and in the Injil and the Qur'an. And like the Christians who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an.

﴿And they want to adopt a way between that﴾ i.e., a middle religion between faith and disbelief, and there is no intermediate position between the two.

Those are the complete disbelievers. They are the perfect ones in disbelief, because disbelief in one (of the messengers) is disbelief in all. "Truly" (ḥaqqan) is an emphasis on the content of the sentence, like your saying: "This is the servant of God, truly," meaning: that is true, truly, namely that they are perfect in disbelief. Or it is an adjective of the verbal noun of "the disbelievers," meaning: they are the ones who disbelieved a true disbelief, firm, certain, with no doubt in it. "And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment" — in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 4, verse 152:

﴿Those who believe in God and His messengers, and do not make distinction between any of them﴾. The use of "bayn" (between) with "aḥad" (any one) is permissible because "aḥad" is general, applying to the singular, masculine and feminine, and their dual and plural forms. (p-411) ﴿He will give them their wages﴾: the reading "yu'tīhim" (with a ya', "he will give them") is from Ḥafṣ, with the word ﴿يُؤْتِيهِمْ﴾ read in this way. ﴿Their wages﴾ means the reward promised to them. ﴿And God is ever Forgiving﴾, who conceals bad deeds, ﴿Merciful﴾, who accepts good deeds.

The verse refutes the position of the Mu'tazila (a theological school) on the eternal punishment of the one who commits a grave sin (*al-kabīra*), because it states that whoever believes in God and His messengers and does not make distinction between any of them will be given his reward. The one who commits a grave sin is among those who believe in God and His messengers and do not make distinction between any of them, so he falls under the promise. The verse also refutes the view of those who do not affirm the eternity (*qidam*) of the attributes of action, such as forgiveness and mercy, because He said: ﴿And God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, while they say: God was not Forgiving and Merciful in eternity, and then became Forgiving and Merciful.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 153:

When Finhas (Phinehas) and his companions said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If you are a truthful prophet, then bring us a Book from heaven all at once, as Musa (peace be upon him) brought," the verse was revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾. It is read with the lightened (tashdid-less) form of tanzil (tukhaffif), by Ibn Kathir (Makki) and Abu 'Amr.

﴿A Book from heaven﴾ means: all at once, just as the Torah was sent down all at once. They proposed this only as a way of obstinate challenge. Al-Hasan said: "Had they asked him in search of guidance, He would have given it to them, because sending down the Qur'an all at once is possible."

﴿So they asked Musa for something greater than that﴾. This is the answer to an implied conditional clause, meaning: "If you consider what they asked of you to be great, then they asked Musa for something greater than that." The asking is attributed to them, though it was done by their forefathers in the days of Musa (peace be upon him), namely the seventy chosen men (al-nuqaba' al-sab'un), because they were of the same creed and approved of their request. ﴿Then they said: "Show us Allah openly"﴾, that is, visibly: "Show us that we may see Him openly."

﴿So the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqah) seized them﴾, meaning the terrible punishment, or the burning fire, ﴿because of their wrongdoing﴾ against themselves by asking for something that was not in its proper place, or by dictating to their Prophet concerning the signs and by their obstinacy in demanding the vision, not because of asking for the vision itself, since it is possible, just as the Qur'an was sent down all at once. (p-412) Had the seizing been because of asking for the vision, Musa would have been more deserving of it, for he said: ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You﴾, and the thunderbolt did not seize him; rather He gave him hope and restricted it to what is possible, and only what is possible of establishment is made conditional on what is possible. Then He revived them. ﴿Then they took the calf﴾ as a god ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾, the Torah and the nine miracles. ﴿Yet We pardoned that﴾ out of grace, and did not uproot them. ﴿And We gave Musa a manifest authority﴾, a clear proof against those who opposed him.

And We raised the Mount above them because of their covenant, so that they would fear [Us] and not break it. ﴿And We said to them,﴾ while the Mount was overshadowing them, ﴿"Enter the gate prostrating."﴾ That is: enter the gate of Iliya' bowing your heads as you enter. ﴿And We said to them, "Do not transgress,"﴾ that is, do not exceed the limit. (تَعَدَّوْا) is read by Warsh, and (تَعْدُّوا), with the ʿayn sukūn and the dāl shaddah, is read by Madani, other than Warsh. Both are an idghām of (تَعْتَدُوا), which is the reading of Ubayy, except that he assimilated the tā' into the dāl and left the ʿayn quiescent in one transmission, while in another transmission he transferred the fatḥah of the tā' onto the ʿayn. ﴿On the Sabbath,﴾ by taking fish. ﴿And We took from them a firm covenant,﴾ a emphatic pledge.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 155:

﴿So for their breaking their covenant﴾ means: "So by their breaking (fa-bi-naqdihim)," and "ma" is redundant (mazidah) for emphasis (lil-tawkid). The "ba'" (bi) is connected to His saying: ﴿We forbade them good things (tayyibat)﴾, its implied sense being: We forbade them good things because of their breaking ﴿their covenant﴾. His saying: ﴿for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews (alladhina hadu)﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying: ﴿for their breaking﴾. The meaning of the emphasis is to affirm that the prohibition of the good things came about only because of the breaking of the covenant, and what is joined to it (ma 'utifa 'alayhi) of disbelief, killing of the prophets, and other things. ﴿And their disbelief in the signs of Allah﴾, that is, the miracles (mu'jizat) of Musa, peace be upon him. ﴿And their killing of the prophets﴾ such as Zakariyya, Yahya, and others.

﴿Without right﴾: without a cause that would make them deserve killing. ﴿And their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered (ghulf)"﴾: ghulf is the plural of aghlaf, meaning veiled, such that nothing of the reminder or admonition reaches them. ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed them over for their disbelief﴾: this is a rejection and denial of their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered." ﴿So they do not believe, except a few﴾ such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

ُ{And because of their disbelief} is conjoined to {for their breaking of the covenant} or to what follows it in His words {because of their disbelief}. Since their disbelief was repeated, for they disbelieved in Musa (Moses), then in Isa (Jesus), then in Muhammad (ﷺ), He conjoined some of their disbelief to some other. {And their saying against Maryam (Mary) a tremendous slander} is the attribution of fornication (zina) to her.

The Masih (the Messiah) was so named because Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, anointed him with blessing, so he is "one who was anointed" (mamsuh). Alternatively, he was named Masih in the sense of "the one who wipes," because he used to wipe over the sick, the blind, and the leper, and they would be healed. Thus he was named Masih with the meaning of al-masih (the one who wipes).

﴿Isa, son of Maryam, the Messenger of Allah.﴾ They did not believe him to be the Messenger of Allah; rather, they said it mockingly, like the words of the disbelievers to our Messenger: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!﴾ It is also possible that Allah described him with this, even though they did not say it.

﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them.﴾ It is narrated that a group of Jews reviled him and reviled his mother. He prayed against them: "O Allah, You are my Lord, and by Your word You created me. O Allah, curse whoever reviled me and reviled my mother." So Allah transformed those who reviled them into apes and swine. The Jews then gathered to kill him. Allah informed him that He would raise him to the heavens and purify him from the company of the Jews. He said to his companions: "Which of you is willing to have my likeness cast upon him, so that he is killed, crucified, and enters Paradise?" A man among them said: "I am." Allah cast his likeness upon him, so he was killed and crucified. It was also said: there was a man who was a hypocrite toward Isa. When they wanted to kill him, he said: "I will show you where he is." He entered Isa's house, Isa was raised, and Allah cast Isa's likeness upon the hypocrite. They entered upon him, killed him, and they thought that he was Isa. This occurred to a people who were obstinate, and Allah's judgment regarding them was that they would not believe.

"Shubbiha" (it was made to appear) is a passive verb whose subject is the prepositional phrase "lahum" (to them), as in your saying: "khuyyila ilayhi" (it was imagined to him). It is as if it were said: "But the appearance of the likeness occurred to them." Or its subject is the pronoun referring to the one who was killed, due to the indication of ﴿Indeed we killed﴾ upon it, as if it were said: ﴿But it was made to appear to them﴾ that the one they killed was (him).

﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾ regarding Isa, meaning the Jews, said: "The face is the face of Isa, but the body is the body of our companion." Or, the Christians differed: some said he is God, and some said he is the son of God, and some said he is the third of three.

﴿They have no knowledge of it, except the following of conjecture.﴾ This is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', an exception whose excluded item is not of the same category as the rest of the sentence), because following conjecture is not of the same kind as knowledge. The meaning is: rather, they follow conjecture. They were described with doubt (shakk), which is that neither of the two sides is preponderant, and then they were described with conjecture (zann), which is that one of them is preponderant, because the intended meaning is that they are in doubt, having no knowledge of it, but if a sign appeared to them, they conjectured accordingly. It was also said: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning him﴾ meaning concerning his killing, ﴿are in doubt about it﴾ meaning about his killing, because they used to say: if this is Isa, then where is our companion? And if this is our companion, then where is Isa?

﴿And they did not kill him with certainty﴾ meaning, a certain killing; or, they did not kill him as those who were certain; or, they did not kill him in truth. Then "with certainty" is made an emphasis for His saying ﴿and they did not kill him﴾, meaning: the negation of his killing is affirmed in truth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 158:

﴿Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ — to a place where no judgment belongs to anyone other than Allah; or, to the heaven. ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾ in His retribution against the Jews, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He arranged of his being raised up to Himself.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 159:

﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but that he will surely believe in him before his death.﴾ "Surely he will believe in him" (la-yu'minanna bihi) is a sentence of oath (jumla qasamiyya) placed as a descriptive clause (sifa) for an omitted antecedent (mawsuf mahdhuf). Its estimated form is: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book﴾ [anyone] ﴿but that he will surely believe in him﴾, and similar to it is: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164]. The meaning: there is none of the Jews and Christians but that he will surely believe before his death in Jesus, peace be upon him, and that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger. That is, when he witnesses it, before his soul departs, at a time when his faith will not benefit him because the time of obligation has ended. Or the pronouns refer to Jesus, meaning: there is none of them but that he will surely believe in Jesus before the death of Jesus, and they are the People of the Book who will be alive at the time of his descent. It is narrated that he will descend from the sky at the end of time, and then none of the People of the Book will remain but that he believes in him, until the religion becomes one, and it is the religion of Islam. Or the pronoun in "bihi" refers to Allah, or to Muhammad (ﷺ), and the second (pronoun) refers to the Book.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them﴾: he will bear witness against the Jews that they denied him, and against the Christians that they claimed him to be the son of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 160:

﴿So for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them﴾. These are what was mentioned in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And to those who became Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ [al-An'am: 146], and so on. The meaning is: We did not forbid them the good things except because of a great wrongdoing they committed, which is what was enumerated before this. ﴿And for their barring many from the way of Allah﴾, that is, preventing them from faith. ﴿Many﴾: that is, a great number of people, or a great deal of barring.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 161:

﴿And their taking of usury, though they had been forbidden from it﴾ Usury (ribā) was forbidden to them just as it has been forbidden to us, and they used to practise it.

﴿And their devouring of people's wealth by falsehood﴾ by bribery and all the other forbidden means. ﴿And We have prepared for the disbelievers among them﴾ other than those who believed, ﴿a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter.

(p. 416)

﴿But those firm in knowledge among them﴾, i.e., those established in it, the God-fearing, such as Ibn Salam and his like. "Those firm in knowledge" is in the nominative by way of inception (*ibtida'*, the grammatical beginning of a nominal sentence). ﴿Among them﴾ means from among the People of the Book, ﴿and the believers﴾, i.e., the believers from among the Emigrants (*Muhajirun*) and the Helpers (*Ansar*). "Those firm in knowledge" is in the nominative by inception, and its predicate (*khabar*) is ﴿believe in what has been sent down to you﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿and what was sent down before you﴾, i.e., the rest of the Books, ﴿and those who establish the prayer﴾, which is in the accusative (*mansub*) by way of praise, to show the excellence of prayer. In the codex (*mushaf*) of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it reads "*wal-muqimun*" (in the nominative), and this is the reading (*qira'a*) of Malik ibn Dinar and others. ﴿And those who give zakat﴾ is a subject (*mubtada'*). ﴿And the believers in God and the Last Day﴾ is conjoined to it, and the predicate is ﴿those — We shall give them a great reward﴾. And with the *ya'* (*sa-yu'tihim*, "He will give them") it is read by Hamza.

"Indeed We have revealed to you" (inna awhayna ilayka) is a reply to the People of the Book concerning their request that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) bring down a book to them from the heaven, and His argument against them that his manner of receiving revelation is like the manner of the earlier prophets, "as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him" (kama awhayna ila Nuhin wal-nabiyyina min ba'dihi), such as Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, and others.

"And We revealed to Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob and the Tribes" (wa awhayna ila Ibrahima wa Isma'ila wa Ishaqa wa Ya'qouba wal-asbati), i.e., the children of Jacob, "and Jesus and Job and Jonah and Aaron and Solomon, and We gave David the Psalms" (wa 'Isa wa Ayyuba wa Yunusa wa Harouna wa Sulayman, wa atayna Dawuda zabura). (Zabūran) is read by Hamzah. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ūl), and the book revealed to David, upon him be peace, was named by it.

{ومُرْسَلاً}... 

Translation:

﴿And messengers﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb having the sense of ﴿We revealed to you﴾, which is "We sent" and "We informed". ﴿Indeed We have related to you before [this] about them﴾ — before this surah. ﴿And messengers We have not related to you﴾.

Abu Dharr asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the prophets, and he said: "They are one hundred and twenty-four thousand." He asked: "How many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and thirteen. The first of the messengers was Adam, and the last of them was your Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)." And four of them were Arabs: Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, and Muhammad (ﷺ).

The verse indicates that knowing the messengers by their individual identities is not a condition for the validity of faith; rather, it is a condition of faith that one believe in them all, for if knowing each one of them were a condition, He would have related all of that to us.

﴿And Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾, that is, without an intermediary.

Qur'an 4:165: "Messengers as bringers of good news and as warners, so that people would have no argument against God after the messengers."

The accusative of "rusulan mubashshirina wa-mundhirina" is best taken as an accusative of praise (al-madh), meaning "I mean: messengers." It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for the first (rusulan of the previous verse), and for it to be an object (maf'ul), meaning "and We sent messengers." The lam in "li-alla yakuna lil-nasi 'ala Allahi hujjatun ba'da al-rusuli" is connected to "mubashshirina wa-mundhirina." The meaning is that their sending removes the excuse and completes the establishment of the argument against them, so that they cannot say: "Why did You not send to us a messenger who would awaken us from the slumber of heedlessness, and alert us to what it is obligatory to be alert to, and teach us what knowledge of is through revelation (al-sam'), such as the acts of worship and the laws (al-shara'i'), namely with regard to their measures, their times, and their modes, but not their foundations, for those are known by reason (bi-l-fi'l)." "And God is ever Mighty" in punishing disbelief in denial, "Wise" in sending messengers as warners.

When the verse ﴿Indeed We have revealed to you﴾ was revealed, they said: "We do not testify to you concerning this." So the verse was revealed: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you.﴾ The meaning of Allah's testifying to what He sent down to him is His affirming its authenticity by manifesting miracles (mu'jizat), just as one establishes claims with proofs, since the Wise does not confirm a liar with a miracle. ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾: that is, He sent it down while knowing that you are fit to receive it and that you will convey it; or He sent it down with what He knew of the interests of the servants. In this there is a refutation of the statement of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who deny the divine attributes, for He affirmed knowledge for Himself.

﴿And the angels bear witness﴾ to your prophethood. ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾: a witness, even if no one else testifies.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 167:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ by denying Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are: the Jews.

﴿and avert [others] from the way of Allah﴾ and prevent people from the way of truth by their saying to the Arabs: "Indeed, we do not find [it] in our Book."

﴿have certainly strayed far astray﴾ from right guidance.

Indeed, those who disbelieved (in Allah) and wronged (Muhammad ﷺ) by altering his description and denying his prophethood.

﴿Allah would never forgive them﴾ so long as they remain upon disbelief.

Translation of the passage:

﴿Nor will He guide them to any path, except the path of Hell, wherein they will abide forever. And that is ever easy for Allah.﴾ Their eternal abiding in Hell is easy for Him. The implied sense is: He will punish them, ﴿abiding forever﴾ — this is a predicative circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah), that is, an abiding that is anticipated, not yet actual at the time of the action. The two verses concern a people whom Allah knew would not believe and would die in disbelief.

O mankind, the Messenger has come to you with the truth from your Lord (ﷺ). That is, with Islam; or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while being truthful.

﴿Believe, it is better for you﴾, and likewise ﴿Desist, it is better for you﴾ [al-Nisa': 171]. Its case-ending (intiṣāb) is governed by a suppressed verb. This is because when he (ﷺ) had urged them to faith and to desisting from the Trinity, he knew that he would be driving them toward a matter, so he said: ﴿better for you﴾. That is: aim for, and adopt, a course better for you than what you are in of disbelief and Trinitarianism, namely: belief in Him and monotheism. ﴿And if you disbelieve, then to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, so your disbelief does not harm Him. ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing﴾ of who believes and who disbelieves, ﴿Wise﴾, who treats them equally in recompense.

O People of the Scripture, do not exceed the limits in your religion. The Jews went to extremes in belittling al-Masih (the Messiah) from his rank, to the point that they said he was the son of adultery, and the Christians went to extremes in elevating him above his measure, by making him the son of Allah. ﴿And do not say about Allah except the truth﴾, which is to declare Him far exalted above having a partner or a son. ﴿The Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, is only the Messenger of Allah﴾, not the son of Allah. ﴿Messenger of Allah﴾ is the predicate of the subject, which is al-Masih, and "Isa" is either an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) or a substitute (badal). ﴿And His word﴾ is conjoined to "Messenger of Allah." It was said that he was called a "word" because he is guided by it, just as one is guided by speech. ﴿Which He conveyed to Maryam﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and "qad" is implied with it, meaning: He delivered it to her and made it attain her.

﴿And a spirit﴾ is also conjoined to the predicate. It was said that he was called a "spirit" because he used to give life to the dead, just as the Qur'an was called a spirit in His saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], because it gives life to hearts. "From Him" means: by His creating and bringing into being, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all of it, from Him﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 13]. With this, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn Waqid answered a Christian slave of al-Rashid who was in his assembly, when the slave claimed that there is a proof in your scripture that Isa is from Allah. ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say "Three."﴾ "Three" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: and do not say the gods are three. ﴿Desist﴾ from the Trinity, ﴿it is better for you.﴾ What the Qur'an indicates, and what they explicitly state, is that Allah, the Messiah, and Maryam are three gods, and that the Messiah is the son of Allah from Maryam. Do you not see His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] and ﴿The Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30]. ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾ is the subject, ﴿is one God﴾ is its predicate, ﴿one﴾ is an emphasis. ﴿Glory be to Him that He should have a son﴾: I glorify Him with glorification, exalting Him above having a son. ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ is an explanation of His transcendence above what is attributed to Him, in the sense that everything in them is His creation and His dominion. How, then, could part of His dominion be a part of Him? For prophethood and dominion do not combine, and the notion of a "part" applies only to bodies, and He is exalted above being a body. ﴿And Allah suffices as a Guardian﴾: a Preserver and Manager of them, and of what is in them. Whoever is unable to suffice in a matter needs a son to help him.

(p-420) [The delegation of Najran said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Why do you disparage our companion Jesus?" He said: "And what should I say?" They said: "Say that he is the servant of Allah and His messenger." He said: "It is no disgrace for him to be a servant of Allah." They said: "Indeed, it is not." Then the words of the Most High were revealed: ﴿The Messiah will not disdain﴾, meaning: will not be too proud, ﴿to be a servant of Allah﴾. This is a rebuttal of the Christians. ﴿Nor the angels﴾, a rebuttal of those among the Arabs who worship them, and it is conjoined to "the Messiah". ﴿Those brought near﴾, meaning the Karubiyyun (the cherubim, those who surround the Throne), such as Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and those of their rank. The meaning is: ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ will disdain to be servants of Allah, and that was omitted, because ﴿a servant of Allah﴾ indicates it, for brevity. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) and those who hold the superiority of the angel over the human clung to this verse and said: "Elevation is only towards what is higher. One says: So-and-so does not disdain to serve me, nor does his father. Had he said: nor his servant, it would not have been well put." So the meaning of His words ﴿nor the angels brought near﴾ is: nor those who are higher than him in rank and greater than him in station. This is indicated by the specification of "those brought near." The reply: We grant that the second is superior to the first, but this does not touch what we dispute, because the verse indicates that all the angels brought near are superior to Jesus, and we grant that all the angels brought near are superior to a single messenger from among humans. This is the view of some of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox Sunni community). Moreover, the intended meaning is that the angels, together with their extraordinary power, their rank, their inspired knowledge, and their being wholly free from procreation by pairing, do not disdain to worship Him. How much more so one who is begotten of another, who does not have the power they have, and does not know what they know?! This is because great might, vast knowledge, and the strangeness of creation are what breed foolishness, like that of the Christians, who conceive of disdaining servitude, since they saw that the Messiah was born without a father, that he healed the blind and the leper, raised the dead, and told them what they eat and store in their houses. So they cleared him of servitude. It was said to them: These attributes are more complete in the angels than in the Messiah, and yet they did not disdain servitude; how then should the Messiah? The conclusion is that the elite of humanity, namely the prophets, peace be upon them, are superior to the elite of the angels, namely the messengers among them, such as Jibril, Mika'il, 'Izra'il, and the like. The elite of the angels are superior to the common believers among humans, and the common believers among humans are superior to the common angels. Our proof for the superiority of humans over the angel, taken at the outset, is that they subdued the impulses of desire for the sake of Allah, the Most High, although they were created with those impulses. Thus the prophets, peace be upon them, resembled the angels, peace be upon them, in infallibility, and surpassed them in overcoming the psychic motives and the bodily drives. So their obedience was harder, since it was accompanied by obstacles, unlike the obedience of the angels, since they were created inclined to it; therefore it carries greater reward. By the saying of Allah: ﴿And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant﴾, through exalting himself and seeking greatness, ﴿He will gather them all to Himself﴾, so that He will recompense them for their disdain and their arrogance. Then he explained, saying:]

(p-421)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 173:

﴿As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty. But as for those who disdain and are arrogant, He will punish them with a painful punishment, and they will find for themselves, besides Allah, no protector and no helper.﴾

If you say: the detailed statement (al-tafsil) does not correspond to what it details (al-mufassal), because the detailed statement includes both groups, while what is detailed concerns only one group. I say: it is like your saying: "The imam gathered the Kharijites (al-Khawarij). Whoever did not rebel against him, he clothed and carried; and whoever rebelled against him, he made an example of." The soundness of this is for two reasons. The first: he omitted mention of one of the two groups because the detailed statement indicates it, and because mention of one of them implies mention of the second, just as he omitted one of them in the detailed statement in His words, exalted is He, after this: ﴿As for those who believe in Allah and hold fast to Him﴾. The second: that benefiting others apart from them is something that grieves them, so it falls within the category of making an example of them. It is as if it were said: whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, he will be tormented with regret when he sees the rewards of those who act, and with what befalls him of the punishment of Allah.

O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord (﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord﴾), that is, His Messenger, who overwhelms the denier with the miracle (of the Qur'an); ﴿And We have sent down to you a clear light﴾, that is, the Qur'an, by which one is guided through the darknesses of bewilderment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 175:

﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him﴾: in Allah, or in the Qur'an. ﴿He will admit them into mercy from Him﴾, i.e., Paradise, ﴿and bounty﴾, i.e., an increase of blessing, ﴿and guide them to Himself﴾, that is, guide them to Allah, or to the bounty, or to His path, ﴿on a straight path﴾. Regarding "ṣirāṭan": it is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, ḥāl) from the omitted mudāf (the omitted noun governed by the construct, mudāf maḥdhūf).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 4, verse 176:

﴿They ask you for a ruling. Say: "Allah gives you a ruling concerning the kalalah (one who leaves neither father nor child)."﴾ Jabir ibn Abdullah said: "I was ill, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited me and said: 'I am a kalalah; how should I dispose of my property?' (p-422) Then it was revealed."

﴿If a man dies﴾: "a man" (imru') is in the nominative, governed by an implied verb that the apparent word explains. The position of ﴿who has no child﴾ is nominative as a qualifier, meaning: if a man dies who has no descendant. By "child" (walad) is meant the son; it is a shared term that applies to both male and female, because a son excludes the sister, whereas a daughter does not exclude her.

﴿And he has a sister﴾, that is, a full sister or a paternal sister. ﴿Then she has half of what he left﴾, that is, the deceased. ﴿And he inherits from her﴾, that is, the brother inherits all of her property, if the matter is reversed regarding her death and his survival after her, ﴿if she has no child﴾, that is, no son, because a son excludes the brother but not the daughter. If you say: a son does not exclude the brother alone, since the father is his counterpart in exclusion, so why did the verse limit itself to the absence of a child? I say: it stated the ruling for the absence of a child, and it left the ruling for the absence of a father to the explanation of the Sunnah, which is his (ﷺ) saying: "Give the shares of the inheritance to their owners, and what remains goes to the nearest male agnate." The father has priority over the brother.

﴿If there are two sisters﴾, that is, if the sisters are two; this is indicated by ﴿And he has a sister﴾. ﴿Then for them two is two-thirds of what he left.﴾ ﴿And if they are siblings﴾, that is, if those who inherit by siblingship are present. The term "siblings" (ikhwah) refers to brothers and sisters, the masculine taking precedence in ruling. ﴿Men and women﴾, males and females, ﴿for the male is the equivalent of the share of two females.﴾ ﴿Allah makes clear to you﴾ the truth, so it is the object of ﴿yubayyin﴾ (makes clear), ﴿lest you go astray﴾, out of dislike that you should go astray.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾, He knows things in their essence before they exist and after.
